results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 66 aligned outline summaries match the controlling ideas of their spec paragraphs in the spec's order (scene, concepts, architecture, in-practice, judging sections, conclusion); the five callouts are apparatus and align to no spec paragraph.

Introduction ¶3 (p03): the outliner's two summaries (definitions; which chapters own related mechanisms) are the two halves of the spec's single controlling idea, the chapter's terms and their boundary; the boundary sentence is scope, not a second argument.
Architecture ¶12 (p30): user-level randomization is a qualification of how the online experiment that defines parity is run, not a second idea; the spec's controlling idea contains both.

In Practice ¶11 (p52): result, gate passed and the other countries following on the same gates form one consequence chain declared in the spec's controlling idea; the clumsy parenthetical in its rollout sentence is recorded under flow_is_followable.

Every paragraph ties to a supporting claim: scene to S1/S2, strategies and seams to S1, catalog to S3, gates and parity to S4, URL material to S5, switches, rollback and progress to S6, and the account case (Architecture ¶8) to S2's one-writer rule.

Each quotation, case, table and figure is introduced or followed by a sentence saying what it shows: Fowler (settled first-order answer), Scout24 and the strategy table (the rule that follows), Marktplaats replay ('Reproducibility beats realism'), the layer table ('The last row is the definition that matters'), the switch table ('A switch is only as good as the data behind it'), the measures table and Adevinta ('so that delay has a visible price'), the parity table ('The overlap line shows why identical results are the wrong target'), and the lead-ins of the wave, progress, trade-off and vertical tables.

All other boundaries express their declared relationship and pick up the declared known information (e.g. 'Yardstick's question needs a vocabulary first', 'Gates and rollback need an architecture in which two systems run at once', 'Group-level decisions prevent these failures', 'These questions test the decisions above'); boundaries at a subheading are carried by the heading where the relationship is sequence.

Declared elaboration carrying 'the second-order questions about gates, search and URLs'. The paragraph opens on the terms without linking them to the questions just posed, so the reader is not told that stage gate, relevance parity and URL migration are the vocabulary for answering when to go back, whether search is good enough and how to keep URLs working.

results.draft_locus: In Practice: Veldmark's Yardstick Exit Plan ¶13
results.quote: During each wave the SEO team watches four numbers per page type and country
results.finding: Declared cause_effect carrying 'the decision not to change URLs'. The paragraph opens on monitoring with no link to the preceding decision, so it does not say that the monitoring tests (or shows the effect of) keeping URLs unchanged.

The terms on does_not_know are given before use: migration stage gate, relevance parity and URL migration in Introduction ¶3; seams in the callouts and Concepts ¶3; Legacy Mimic, transitional architecture and feature parity in Concepts ¶4-¶8; shadow, parallel run and canary in the mode table; points of no return in In Practice ¶8. Terms both flow readers found unexplained (Seeing Double, A8/B6; Hearthly and Supply Contract v1, A11/B10; VAS and Tally, B5) are on audience.already_knows (failure-pattern names, the brands, Supply Contract v1, VAS, Tally), so they are not failures for the declared reader.
Opens on an intriguing example (Yardstick still shipping every team's work, three days for a fraud rule, 140 engineers on one deploy) and a disputable claim; none of the weak patterns.

The conclusion synthesizes (reversibility until a recorded decision), recalls rather than introduces evidence, gives a course of action and hands off; it does not open with 'in conclusion' or end on a restated thesis.
'every step stays reversible until a recorded decision ends it' is stated by no single section, and 'That bounds the liquidity the move puts at risk' answers why it matters.
'which was the opening's question' returns explicitly to the opening's 'the only choice is how much liquidity it puts at risk', answered with Yardstick's numbers.

The cold reader predicted the sections in order (inventory and dates, vocabulary with the three owned terms, architecture for two systems, Yardstick Exit's insertion and search waves, the judging sections), the evidence (strangler-fig literature, dated classifieds migrations, Google's guidance, fictional Veldmark retiring Yardstick by end 2029) and the tone.

The reader replaced the proposal with slices behind seams (edge, BFFs, CDC), read paths first and system of record last, behavior catalogs, one writer with a Legacy Mimic writer, five gates with numbers agreed in advance and rehearsed rollback, a recorded point of no return, stable URLs, an index rebuilt from the event stream and layered parity gated on non-inferior contacts, not overlap. Only slice ownership by a target-organization team is not mentioned; the core of the expected answer is present.

Chose incremental re-architecture with a lift of the remainder kept as a contingency, justified by the chapter's rule (data model blocks the target) and ruled out a big-bang rewrite, matching Yardstick's plan.

Advised not changing URLs on cut-over, keeping identifiers stable (continuing the legacy sequence), routing by pattern at the edge, a redirect registry with direct 301/308 redirects kept at least a year, new sitemaps, unchanged 410/404 status codes and monitoring of indexed pages, crawl errors and organic traffic.

results.quote: Yardstick has both problems — a co-located data center with a fixed end date, and a 214-column table that blocks every bounded context — which is why its plan strangles the core slice by slice
results.finding: Both readers re-read this: the rule just stated has two branches and Yardstick meets both, but the sentence does not say why the data-model problem decides for re-architecture and reduces re-platforming to a contingency; 'a lift of whatever is left' is also not tied to re-platforming. The spec's order is fine; the prose leaves the decisive reason implicit.
